---
argmap-version: 0.2
title: "Tutorial: explicates vs replaces (when a pin is allowed)"
description: "The same claim, the same two grounds and the same step, written twice, differing only in indentation. In the first block the support sits INSIDE the claim's own block, which explicates the number the author put on it, so the pin stays. In the second the support sits beside the claim as a sibling line, which replaces the author's number, so the pin comes off and a `# check:` takes its place. This is D36's residual rule and it is the distinction every one of the older examples in this directory gets wrong: a pin plus incoming support is an author quietly arguing with their own evidence, and the solve cannot tell you which half they meant."
---

# ===========================================================================
# THE KEEPER SENTENCE, from the authoring skill:
#
#     A statement's own indented block EXPLICATES its number;
#     sibling lines concluding into it REPLACE it.
#
# So the test is not "does anything conclude into this claim". It is "where
# does the thing concluding into it live". Indented under the claim: keep the
# pin, the block is telling the reader why the author believes it. At the
# same level as the claim: take the pin off, because the lines are now doing
# the believing and a pin would double-count.
#
# The frontier roots keep their pins in both blocks, because nothing at all
# concludes into them. That never changes.
#
# WHY THE RULE EXISTS, in one line: a pin is a constraint and so is an
# incoming line, so a claim carrying both is two constraints fighting, and
# the solve splits the difference in a way no reader can interpret. The
# `# check:` comment is the escape: it records the author's own number where
# a reader and a solver readout can both see it, and keeps it OUT of the
# solve, so the gap between it and the solved value is an audit finding
# rather than a compromise.
# ===========================================================================

# ---- block 1: EXPLICATES. The support is in the claim's own block. --------
# @safe keeps its pin. The two grounds and the step below it are inside the
# claim's block, which is the author showing their working for a number they
# are standing behind.

@safe [The footbridge is safe to reopen] 0.8: the pin stays, and everything under this line is here to explain it
  @load [The load test met the design margin] 0.9:
  @cracks [No new cracks appeared over the winter] 0.85:
  $eng [test plus inspection is what the standard asks for] 0.9 @safe | @load AND @cracks:

# ---- block 2: REPLACES. The same support, one indent level out. -----------
# Identical content, identical numbers, and the pin is gone. $eng2 is a
# sibling of @safe2, not part of it, so it is the lines that assert the
# claim now. The author's own 0.8 moves into a `# check:` comment.

@safe2 [The footbridge is safe to reopen]:  # check: 0.8
@load2 [The load test met the design margin] 0.9:
@cracks2 [No new cracks appeared over the winter] 0.85:
$eng2 [test plus inspection is what the standard asks for] 0.9 @safe2 | @load2 AND @cracks2:

# ---- the readout ----------------------------------------------------------
# Solved 2026-08-04 (D36 defaults, solve_map.py). The two blocks share every
# number, so any difference between them is the placement and nothing else.
#
#   block 1   @safe   0.80       -> 0.801     @load 0.893   @cracks 0.844
#   block 2   @safe2  check 0.80 -> 0.833     @load2 0.893  @cracks2 0.844
#
# Read the two right-hand columns against each other. In block 1 the pin is
# a live constraint and it holds the claim almost exactly where the author
# put it. In block 2 nothing holds it, so the step carries it up on its own,
# and the small gap from 0.80 is the audit finding: the author's summary
# judgment was a little more cautious than their own two grounds warrant.
#
# HONEST FOOTNOTE, because it is the first thing a careful reader asks. The
# solver has no special rule for a statement's own block: $eng is an ordinary
# evidence concluding into @safe, and the pin is an ordinary floor pair, so
# mechanically both constrain. The distinction taught here is an AUTHORING
# one, and it earns its keep because it answers "whose number is this": in
# block 1 the author is standing behind 0.8 and showing why, in block 2 the
# author is standing behind the grounds and letting the number fall out.
# (D38's replace rule is a different thing and applies to a refined EVIDENCE,
# not to a statement's block; t1-refinement is the file for that.)
#
# The one place the two readings collide: a HINGE statement deep inside an
# evidence's refinement, with lines concluding into it from within that same
# refinement, takes a check and not a pin (AUTHORING_TUTORIAL 4.2). If the
# source also asserts the hinge outright, write that assertion as its own
# premise-less attributed evidence rather than as a pin, so it accumulates
# with the argued routes instead of clamping over them.
#
# What the wrong version would look like: put `0.8` back on @safe2 while
# leaving $eng2 where it is, and the file now says two incompatible things
# about the same claim with no way to tell which the author meant. The lint
# will not stop you. Nothing will. This is a discipline, not a check, which
# is exactly why it is worth a tutorial file of its own.
#
# One consequence worth carrying away: in a real map most claims are
# concluded into, so most claims carry no pin. A map full of pins is usually
# a map whose author authored their conclusions and then went looking for
# reasons.
